title: The Peculiar Problem of Perpetual Pleasure
text:
We have peripherals that stream signals into us, and an internal reality that emerges from them. How much of this reality is a function of the stream, and how much is a function of the mechanism that interprets it?
If all we experience of life is this internal reality, why not learn to control it?
Take sex. What if all of us could remain in a state of orgasmic pleasure forever?
Assume the sensation could be sustained indefinitely, without habituation. Would that be an ideal existence?
The system has no dynamics: no anticipation, no longing, no discovery.
Imagine a creator designing a mechanism for experiencing reality. He identifies what appears to be the highest state of pleasure and creates avatars fixed there forever.
But how can he know that this is the highest possible state? What if he has merely found a local optimum?
By fixing the state of his avatars, he ends the experiment.
What should he do instead?
He could give them agency, introduce uncertainty, and let them explore the space of possible experiences. Perhaps they encounter states of being that the creator himself had not conceived of.
We spend our lives trying to gain more control over our experiences. Yet falling in love or stumbling upon a beautiful idea derives part of its pleasure from being outside our control.
What if the objective is not to maximize pleasure at every instant, but to maximize the capacity to discover new kinds of pleasure?
I wonder whether our present condition, with its peculiar balance of agency and uncertainty, is closer to an optimal design than we think.

title: Diversify Your Identity
text:
Under uncertainty, diversification is rational. Success often requires concentrated effort. Can I concentrate effort while diversifying identity?
It occurred to me that I watch more films, across a wider range, than some self-proclaimed movie buffs. Yet I do not derive the same pride from it.
Identification adds a form of gratification beyond the activity itself.
A casual moviegoer becomes a discerning cinephile. A coffee drinker becomes a coffee connoisseur. The activities change less than one’s relationship with them.
Much of my identity comes from my intellectual and professional pursuits. This makes my sense of self unnecessarily fragile. A single variable explains too much of its variance.
What if I could concentrate effort along one axis while deriving satisfaction from several?
There is a risk of going too far. I could turn photography, something I enjoy, into another axis along which to feel inadequate.
Perhaps the trick is to take pride in how I engage with something without tying too much pride to how good I am at it.
Concentrate effort. Diversify identity.

title: Psychedelic Experience
text:
There was a sense of knowing stronger than anything I had felt before. It began with mild anxiety. I tried to ignore it. Then the blanket became dancing animals.
I was in bed between two dark curtains. A lighter curtain in the middle let in enough light to make me want to look outside, but I could not, or it no longer seemed important.
Drinking water became an engineering problem. I pulled the bottle toward me, opened it, held the top, and lifted the bottom. I had to push the bottle down with my mouth to tilt it. I had the strength of a two-year-old.
My chest began moving vigorously back and forth, as if I were possessed. The movement felt both voluntary and compelled. I was not scared, only surprised. Soon it was accompanied by hysterical laughter.
Then came more realizations than I could process. Whether any were true, I cannot say. The certainty was part of the experience. It felt as if my mind were expanding faster than it could represent what was happening.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Successful outcomes are easy to explain backward. We see skill and effort because they are visible. Luck disappears into the story.
Starting early does not defeat luck. It buys more attempts. More attempts mean more failures one can survive and more chances to notice what works. Time is not just a resource; it is sample size.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Intensity is trainable
Absorption is not merely a personality trait. A craft, practiced without interruption, makes sustained attention easier to enter. Repetition builds familiarity with the state itself: how to begin, how to stay, and how to return after distraction.
The useful skill is not permanent intensity. It is the ability to direct intensity when the work requires it.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Approval is expensive
When work requires approval from everyone around me, quality becomes secondary. The objective quietly changes from making something good to avoiding disagreement.
Disagreement need not be hostile. It means refusing to outsource decisions that determine the shape of my work or life.

title: Notes on Building Things
section: Build a system small enough to repeat
text:
Build a system small enough to repeat
Large goals are global objectives. Days are local updates. A routine connects the two.
If the daily update is too large, an ordinary interruption breaks the system. A smaller commitment produces less progress today but survives more days. Its advantage appears only after accumulation.
Consistency and ambition are not opposites. Ambition chooses the direction. Consistency keeps applying the update.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Find the constraint
Complex projects do not advance evenly. Usually one unresolved problem blocks the rest. Doing ten available tasks can feel productive while leaving that constraint untouched.
The useful question is not “What can I finish today?” It is “What is preventing the project from moving?” Breaking that problem into a task small enough for one day is often the real work.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Work close to feedback
A salary is not the problem. Distance from feedback can be. Work becomes dull when action is separated from consequence and nothing accumulates: not skill, ownership, judgment, or leverage.
Startups are not automatically better, nor are large organizations automatically worse. The better questions are: How quickly can I see what my work changed? Am I learning something scarce? Does the value I create compound beyond the hours I spend?

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Choose the environment
Part of luck is exposure. A place changes the people one meets, the problems one sees, and the standards that feel normal.
Discomfort is useful when it reveals a limit. It is not useful merely because it hurts. The right environment makes complacency difficult without making sustained work impossible.

title: Notes on Building Things
section: Treat fear as a noisy signal
text:
Treat fear as a noisy signal
Fear is neither a command nor an enemy. It is a noisy risk detector. When it appears, I can ask what failure it predicts, how likely that failure is, and whether the downside can be reduced.
Sometimes the signal identifies a real flaw. Sometimes it protects the familiar. The task is to tell the two apart.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Ideas need not be original
Two reliable sources of ideas are problems I repeatedly face and solutions that work elsewhere.
The first comes with evidence: I know the problem exists. A useful test is whether I would pay for a solution. The second is a form of pattern matching. A model that works in one industry or country may work under different constraints after adaptation.
Copying the surface is easy. Understanding the mechanism is the creative part.

title: Notes on Building Things
text:
Attention reveals the objective
Attention is finite. News, messages, work, and entertainment continually bid for it. The things that repeatedly win become my objective function in practice, regardless of what I claim to value.
When my stated goals and observed attention disagree, my behavior is the more accurate description.

title: Introspection
text:
The nearest things to my control are attention and action. Other people remain partly hidden. I can observe what they do and infer what they think, but I cannot access their minds directly.
Much avoidable suffering comes from ignoring this boundary. I act, then quietly treat the response I want as part of the action. When reality returns something else, I experience the difference as a violation.
Can action exist without an expected result? Probably not completely. But expectation can be held as a prediction rather than a contract.

title: Introspection
text:
Mental states
Achievement, grief, desire, and boredom are different mental states produced under different conditions. Much of life is spent arranging conditions that produce some states and avoid others.
This raises a practical question: how much control comes from changing the conditions, and how much comes from changing how I meet them?

title: Introspection
text:
Now
Every future I imagine, if it arrives, will arrive as a present moment. Memory also happens now. So do anticipation, dread, and the physical pain in front of me.
This sounds obvious, yet my mind keeps treating the present as a corridor to somewhere else. If experience is only ever available now, the capacity to attend may matter as much as the conditions being attended to.
Could I be joyful without first acquiring a person, object, belief, or future? I do not know. It would be useful to find out.

title: Introspection
text:
Discovery
Life looks inefficient in retrospect. I spend time on work, ideas, and relationships that later seem to have produced nothing.
But the judgment uses information that was unavailable when I made the choice. Trial and error looks wasteful only after the error is known. I cannot act with the awareness of my future self.
Regret may still contain information. It should update the next choice, not pretend the previous one was obvious.

title: Introspection
text:
Love and competition
Good intentions toward another person do not require agreement or passivity. I can play football to win while wanting my opponent to leave the field uninjured. The game is zero-sum; the relationship need not be.
Trouble begins when winning becomes the only available source of joy. Then another person’s success is not merely their gain. It becomes evidence of my loss.

title: Introspection
text:
Belief and doubt
Belief reduces cognitive load. It compresses many decisions into a rule and makes coordination with a group easier. Doubt reopens those decisions and demands more work.
Neither is sufficient alone. A person who doubts everything cannot act. A person who doubts nothing cannot update. The useful balance may depend on the cost of being wrong and the cost of waiting.

title: Introspection
text:
Dissatisfaction
Dissatisfaction creates motion. The present state differs from an imagined one, and action tries to close the gap.
The mechanism is useful, but it has no natural stopping condition. Reaching one target changes the reference point and produces another gap. If dissatisfaction is the only source of movement, the future keeps consuming the present it was meant to improve.

text:
Applied Scientist | Distributed Training and Foundation Models


  X









I build foundation-model systems. At Amazon Prime Video, I work on foundation models for recommender systems.

Earlier, I built low-latency conversational AI systems at Vox AI and production deep reinforcement learning systems for quantitative trading at Niveshi.

Implemented model and training components across tensor parallelism, sequence parallelism, multi-objective training, and checkpoint loading for Amazon Nova multimodal models.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Intention describes what I choose to do. Expectation describes what I think should happen in return. They often travel together, but I control the first more than the second.
Confusing them turns every action into a wager whose emotional payoff depends on circumstances I do not control.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Intention describes what I choose to do. Expectation describes what I think should happen in return. They often travel together, but I control the first more than the second.
Confusing them turns every action into a wager whose emotional payoff depends on circumstances I do not control.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Validation
Wanting acknowledgment is not a flaw. We are social animals; inclusion matters. The problem begins when external approval becomes the only measurement that counts.
Awareness does not remove the desire for validation. It makes the dependency visible.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Watching the mind
Thoughts appear, associate, and disappear, often without instruction. Observing that process changes my relation to it. A thought can be present without becoming an order, a belief, or an identity.
That small gap is easy to miss. It may be the beginning of choice.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Experience as evidence
Some questions cannot be answered from a distance. Curiosity about travel is better tested by traveling. Curiosity about meditation is better tested by sitting still for a day.
Direct experience supplies data that thought alone cannot. It is evidence, not a conclusion.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Impermanence
Almost none of my body or mental content is the same as it was a decade ago. Memory stitches these changing states into a continuous self.
Continuity need not be an illusion to be a construction. Seeing how it is built loosens the need to defend every current belief as a permanent part of me.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Desire and happiness
Fulfilling a desire often produces satisfaction, but usually not for long. Another desire appears, or the new condition becomes ordinary.
This does not make desire bad. It means happiness cannot be modeled as a finite queue that, once cleared, leaves a permanent state. The system generates new items while processing the old ones.
Can joy exist without first requiring the world to change?

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Education
We measure education through information and skill because both are easy to test. Education could also expand attention, the ability to examine one’s desires, and the capacity to disagree without treating disagreement as a threat.
Those outcomes are harder to measure, so they are easier to ignore.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Identity
Beliefs compress experience into a usable model of the world and of myself. The model becomes a problem when new evidence feels like an attack.
A stable identity lowers the cost of everyday decisions. It can also raise the cost of changing my mind.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Discipline
Discipline is repeated allocation of time toward a chosen direction. Its value is practical, not moral. A routine reduces the number of decisions between intention and action.
Small repetitions are difficult to evaluate because their effects appear later. That delay makes consistency easy to underestimate.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Simplicity
When an experience becomes confusing, it helps to describe the facts before explaining them. What happened? What did I feel? What did I want? What am I afraid will happen next?
The story may still be necessary. It should come after observation, not replace it.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Choosing a direction
Imagining an ideal day, work environment, relationship, or state of health is not prophecy. It produces constraints. A direction becomes useful only when it changes the next action.
Action then returns information and updates the model. Without that feedback, an ideal life can remain a collection of desires imported from other people.

title: Collected Thoughts
text:
Anger
Anger narrows attention. One interpretation of events begins to feel complete, and alternatives disappear.
Observing the physical sensations may not end the anger, but it can reintroduce choice. The question is not whether awareness and anger can coexist. It is whether there is enough awareness to decide what happens next.

title: A desire is not a decision
text:
A desire and an action are different events. I can want something without doing it. But if I refuse to admit the desire, I lose the chance to choose clearly.
Jealousy, sexual desire, hunger for status, or the urge to avoid difficult work can arrive before I have a theory about them. Then culture and self-image label the feeling good or bad. Shame begins when the feeling conflicts with the person I think I should be.
This does not make every drive wise. Some actions harm others; some harm me. Acceptance is not permission. It is accurate observation: this impulse exists. What happens next remains a decision.
Cultures disagree about which desires deserve shame. That variation suggests that at least some guilt is learned. A more useful question than “Should a good person feel this?” is: “What is this drive asking for, and what would happen if I acted on it?”
A drive seen clearly can be examined. A drive hidden behind a moral story still influences behavior, but without scrutiny. I suspect awareness gives us slightly more control, not by removing the drive, but by separating it from action.

title: The Thread of Higher Knowledge
text:
There always seems to be a thread of higher knowledge hanging above us. We can climb it and operate at a higher level of abstraction.
I have been developing an interest in cinematography. A movie is no longer only a story. I notice the composition, the movement of the camera, the use of light, and the choices made in withholding information from the viewer.
The same movie, viewed by the same person at two points in their intellectual life, becomes two different experiences.
The world does not need to change for one’s experience of it to change.
Knowledge increases the resolution at which one experiences reality.
I could drink coffee every morning for the next forty years. Or I could gradually understand its origins, the differences between beans, and the process that turns them into what I taste.
The physical act remains largely the same. The internal experience becomes richer.
Occasionally, climbing one thread of knowledge brings several others into view that were previously invisible.
Perhaps living a richer life is as much about increasing one’s capacity to experience things as it is about increasing the number of things one experiences.
Not merely seeing more of the world, but seeing more in it.
